items.text: Term life insurance covers a set number of years, then ends. Whole life is permanent and builds cash value, at a higher premium. Neither is automatically better - the right one depends on what the coverage actually needs to do. (571) 354-0146

"Should I get term or whole life?" is one of the most common questions we get, and the honest answer is that it depends on the job the policy needs to do.

Term life covers you for a fixed period, commonly 10 to 30 years, and pays a benefit only if you die within that term. It carries no cash value. It is generally the lower-cost way to cover a specific need with an end date - a mortgage, income replacement while children are young, a business loan.

Whole life is permanent. Coverage does not expire as long as premiums are paid, and part of the premium builds cash value you can borrow against or, in some cases, use to offset premiums later. That permanence and the cash value come at a materially higher premium than term for the same benefit amount.

Neither is objectively better. Term fits a need with a natural end date. Whole life fits a need that does not end - final expenses, an inheritance you want to guarantee, or a policy meant to last regardless of when you die.

We walk through which category actually matches what you are trying to accomplish before talking about specific policies.

Term or whole life insurance - which one actually fits? Term covers a set number of years and costs less, built for a need with an end date like a mortgage or years with kids at home. Whole life is permanent and builds cash value, at a higher premium, built for a need that doesn't expire.
